sections.label: THINKING
sections.content:
The yellow core never moves (always (20,24)). Arrow keys always move the green core (regardless of which frame I click). In other words, there's only one movable player (the green core), and the yellow core is static.
Interesting point: after "clickGframe" + RIGHT, the green core didn't move (stayed at (40,12)). But after "clickYframe" + RIGHT, it moved from (40,10)→(40,12). And after "clickYcore" + RIGHT, it didn't move (stayed at (40,12)).
Wait, this is strange. Let me look again:
- Start: green (40,10).
- clickYframe (18,22), RIGHT → green (40,12). Moved.
- clickGframe (38,8), RIGHT → green (40,12). Didn't move!
- clickYcore (20,24), RIGHT → green (40,12). Didn't move!
So the green core moved after clicking the yellow frame, but didn't move after clicking the green frame or the yellow core. This is bizarre. Could it be... that the arrow keys move the core of the container that isn't the one clicked? Or maybe there's a "hover" mechanism: the last MOUSE position is the hover, and the arrow keys move the core of the container under the hover... but (38,8) is the green container, (20,24) is the yellow core, (18,22) is the yellow frame.
After clicking (18,22) [yellow frame], RIGHT moved the green core.
After clicking (38,8) [green frame], RIGHT didn't move the green core.
After clicking (20,24) [yellow core], RIGHT didn't move the green core.
This doesn't fit a simple "hover" model either.
Wait, maybe the movement is blocked by the piece state! The green core is at (40,12) = the right edge of the container. RIGHT from (40,12) is blocked (it's the edge). So "RIGHT after Gframe" and "RIGHT after Ycore" didn't move because the core was already at the right edge (40,12) and RIGHT is blocked!
And "RIGHT after Yframe" moved from (40,10) to (40,12) (not blocked).
So the arrow keys always move the green core, and it's currently at the right edge (40,12). That makes sense! The yellow core is static.
Okay, so there's only one player: the green core, 9 positions. The yellow core is static decoration (or a "key" that's always present).
Now, let me systematically sweep all 36 combinations (9 positions × 4 piece states). The timer is lenient. Let's do it.
Current: green (40,12), red A, blue 1.
Plan: for each of the 4 piece states, sweep the 9 core positions.
To sweep the 9 positions from any starting point, I can use a fixed movement sequence that visits all 9. The core's top-left is at rows {38,40,42}, columns {8,10,12}. Let me define the positions:
(38,8)=P0, (38,10)=P1, (38,12)=P2
(40,8)=P3, (40,10)=P4, (40,12)=P5
(42,8)=P6, (42,10)=P7, (42,12)=P8
Movement (2 cells per key): from a position, UP/DOWN changes the row by 2 (38↔40↔42), LEFT/RIGHT changes the column by 2 (8↔10↔12).
A sequence that visits all 9: start from P5 (40,12).
LEFT→P4(40,10), LEFT→P3(40,8), UP→P0(38,8), RIGHT→P1(38,10), RIGHT→P2(38,12), DOWN→P5(40,12), DOWN→P8(42,12), LEFT→P7(42,10), LEFT→P6(42,8).
That visits P5,P4,P3,P0,P1,P2,P5,P8,P7,P6 — all 9 (P5 twice).
So from P5: [LEFT,LEFT,UP,RIGHT,RIGHT,DOWN,DOWN,LEFT,LEFT] visits all 9.
For each piece state:
1. Set the piece state (up to 2 clicks).
2. Move to P5 if not there (or start from the current position).
3. Execute the 9-visit sequence, checking after each move.
Let me structure it:
- State A,1 (current): the core is at P5. Execute the sequence, checking at each of the 9 positions.
- Then set to A,0 (blue click). The core is now at P6 (42,8). I need to return to P5: from P6: RIGHT→P7, RIGHT→P8, UP→P5. Then execute the sequence.
- Then set to B,0 (red click). The core is at P6. Return to P5, execute the sequence.
- Then set to B,1 (blue click). The core is at P6. Return to P5, execute the sequence.
This is 4 states × (about 3 return moves + 9 sequence moves + 1 click) ≈ 4×13 = 52 actions. A lot, but the timer is lenient (currently step 87, bar about 22; the limit is probably 256).
Actually, let me reduce: after the sequence, the core ends at P6. To return to P5 from P6: RIGHT, RIGHT, UP (3 moves). No problem.
Let me write the code with a win check after each move. Stop if there's a win.
Let me define the sequence and execute it.
